blindSummary:
Trans visitors face severe risk here. A colonial-era penal-code provision criminalises same-sex intimacy, and police use "shadow laws" — notably a provision of an 1899 colonial municipal police law allowing detention of anyone who cannot "satisfactorily account" for themselves — to target trans and gender-nonconforming people. Since the February 2021 coup the situation has turned lethal: the opposition government-in-exile has documented 17 LGBT people killed by mid-2022, and rights groups document arrests, torture, and sexual abuse of LGBT people by the military government's forces, with the 2024 conscription law falling brutally on queer people.

In 2025 the military government banned seven books for LGBTQ+ content as "obscene." There is no legal gender recognition, no protection of any kind, and no institutional recourse — police and military are the primary predators. Resistance-controlled areas are nominally friendlier but are active war zones.

For a visitor: any visible gender nonconformity risks detention under the police-law powers, with torture documented in custody; the general security collapse compounds everything.
blindOutOfScope: General civil-war risks affect all travellers and are out of scope; this record concerns only trans-specific persecution by the military government.
blindTangential: The colonial-era penal-code sodomy provision criminalises same-sex intimacy — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the police-law "shadow law" is the trans-specific detention mechanism.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): the colonial-era penal-code provision criminalises same-sex intimacy, reinforced by 'shadow laws' and police discretion (e.g. a provision of an 1899 colonial municipal police law used to detain people who cannot 'satisfactorily account' for their presence). Since the February 2021 coup, risks have intensified sharply - abuses in interrogation and detention reflecting homophobia, transphobia and punitive sexual violence; a UN special rapporteur warns of widespread sexual and gender-based violence against women, girls and LGBTQ people.

Diaspora news outlet (Jan 2024): LGBT discrimination on the rise since the 2021 coup - attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse by authorities; the opposition government-in-exile's human-rights ministry stated 17 LGBT people were killed and two critically injured since Feb 2021; first-person accounts from trans women protesters.

National human-rights organisation's submission (June 2024) to a UN special rapporteur on extrajudicial executions: killing of LGBTIQ+ persons in military-controlled areas of this country - 5 to 12 individuals dead since the coup; enforcement of the colonial-era sodomy provision intensified as an aggravating factor; militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life.

Overseas broadcaster (Jan 2025): the military government banned seven books with LGBTQ+ themes and will take legal action against their publishers, calling them 'obscene' and socially unacceptable - part of the community's long oppression in a broadly conservative society.

Regional LGBT-rights coalition report (March 2025): this country's LGBTQIA+ community under the shadow of the 2024 conscription law, based on research by an advocacy group led by exiles from this country; the law has forced queer individuals into a cycle of fear, discrimination and oppression, with legal frameworks stripping identity (conscripted people are processed by gender assigned at birth and forced into uniforms).
Foreign broadsheet (Feb 2016): trans activists organising in the country's largest city despite colonial-era laws and police abuse.
LGBT-rights outlet (Nov 2018): a gay man with HIV was charged under this country's colonial-era sodomy law - demonstrating active enforcement of the colonial-era criminalisation.

News site (Oct 2015): feature on why gay people in this country cannot live openly, part of a 10-part series on LGBT rights across the country's region; documents the 2013 case in a provincial city where trans women were allegedly forced to strip in public by police; notes a traditional spirit-medium role in local folk religion historically occupied by trans women and cross-dressing men.
